entries.title: Trump Says He'd 'Love' to See a Unified Ireland
entries.summary: "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," the president said during meetings in Dublin.
entries.content:
DUBLIN (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course.

At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the U.K.’s Northern Ireland.

“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.

“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”

The Irish unity debate is heated

Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it's Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous American presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong emotional ties to Ireland.

When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbor Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.

Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles: three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.

A 1998 peace accord that the U.S. was instrumental in striking largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.

The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that “I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one.”

Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands issue

Trump again raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falkland Islands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated Argentina’s claim to the islands, a British overseas territory that Argentina calls Las Malvinas.

Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the South Atlantic islands as they did after Argentina invaded in 1982.

“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.

A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump

Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address U.S. and Irish business leaders at the U.S. ambassador's official residence in Dublin, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open.

Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”

The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the U.S. national anthem and inspected an Irish Army honor guard.

Trump visit irks some Dubliners

Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where he met Connolly at her residence, Áras an Uachtaráin. He met Martin, the taoiseach, at the government’s Farmleigh state guesthouse and stopped by Deerfield, the U.S. ambassador's residence.

Some residents expressed annoyance over the disruption.

“He’s causing mayhem in this city because he wants to go down to Doonbeg and play golf,” said taxi driver Christopher Fox, emphatically not a fan of Trump. “The world’s in turmoil and this fella’s down playing golf.”

University student Mina Petrovski said Trump’s “attitudes toward women, toward immigrants, toward minority communities in general are abhorrent.” She said it’s “shameful that the Irish government is welcoming him with open arms.”

Separately, a collection of left-leaning opposition parties, anti-military groups, pro-Palestinian organizations, environmentalists and others plan to demonstrate against Trump in Dublin on Saturday.

Eric Trump defends family's presence in Ireland

Trump's son, Eric, says the family is loved in Ireland, despite the protests planned over his father's visit.

Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, home to the Trump International golf resort, Eric Trump said the course is the largest employer in the area.

“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them,” he said.

Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

Trump plays golf just about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.

entries.title: Nationals 4, Angels 3: Game Recap
entries.summary: The Nats ended a seven-game losing streak in their Sept. 11 game against Los Angeles.
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

Jorbit Vivas hit a tiebreaking two-run double in the eighth inning to lift Washington to a 4-3 victory over the Los Angeles Angels that snapped the Nationals' seven-game losing streak Friday night.

The Angels led 2-1 before pinch-hitter Andrew Pinckney tied it with a sacrifice fly off Samy Natera Jr. (1-2) in the eighth. Then Vivas hit a flyball that dropped into the corner in right field to make it 4-2.

Clayton Beeter (6-5) won in relief, and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his second save. Tolman allowed an RBI double by Christian Moore that very nearly cleared the wall in right-center for a tying homer, but it stayed in the park and the left-hander retired pinch-hitter Kyren Paris on a flyball to end it.

Mike Trout homered for the first time in over a month for Los Angeles.

Trout hadn't gone deep since Aug. 10 against Texas, but after 27 consecutive homerless games, he connected off Cade Cavalli in the first inning to put the Angels up 1-0.

After a pair of walks in the fourth put men on first and second, James Wood delivered a two-out single that tied the game at 1.

It stayed that way until the seventh, when Cavalli walked the first two hitters and Moore followed with an RBI single to left, chasing the Washington starter. Cavalli allowed two runs, three hits and two walks in six-plus innings, striking out nine.

After Washington started its half of the eighth with a walk and a single, Crews ended up with a bunt single when Natera fielded the ball but turned toward third, where he had no play.

Yohandy Morales followed with a grounder to short, but rather than concede the tying run and try for a double play up the middle, Zach Neto threw home for the force. Pinckney, who was recalled from Triple-A Rochester when the Nationals put infielder Nasim Nuñez on the bereavement list, hit a flyball deep enough to score the tying run.

entries.title: Immigration Group Sues Trump Admin Over Maryland Arrests
entries.summary: The lawsuit details the personal stories of four Maryland residents who have been arrested by ICE in recent months.
entries.content:
An immigrant rights advocacy group filed a lawsuit this week against the Department of Homeland Security on behalf of four Maryland residents who want to stop what they say are unlawful arrests by immigration agents.

We Are CASA, a national group headquartered in Maryland, said the four residents represent all the people in Maryland who have been arrested on alleged immigration violations without a warrant or reason to suspect they are in the country illegally. Two of the residents represented in the lawsuit were arrested in Silver Spring, the others in Annapolis and Eastern Shore.

The group also asked for an injunction to stop Immigration and Customs Enforcement from performing warrantless arrests while the courts weigh the case.

ICE has employed “disturbing tactics” to make arrests, such as smashing car windows and using unmarked vehicles to tail people, as the Trump administration seeks to deport “as many immigrants as possible,” according to the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court in Baltimore.

Government records compiled by the Deportation Data Project, a collaboration between University of California Berkeley and the University of California Los Angeles, show more than 4,900 ICE arrests were made in Maryland in 2025, the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term. The year before, ICE made less than 1,500 arrests in the state.

“These agents have indiscriminately stalked neighborhoods, arresting community members whom they perceive to be Brown or Black immigrants without warrants and without probable cause. This is racial profiling,” Shana Khader, We Are CASA’s legal director, said in a statement.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to The Sun that immigration officers target people who are unlawfully in the U.S., not specific skin colors, races or ethnicities. It called allegations otherwise “disgusting, reckless and categorically FALSE.”

The 56-page lawsuit details the personal stories of the four Maryland residents, who are some of thousands who have been targeted by ICE in recent months. Three of them are identified only by their initials. The complaint recounts the details of their arrests and subsequent release from ICE custody, with accusations of tasings, beatings and failure to properly establish reason for arrest.

Several more advocacy groups are co-counsels on the case, including the Amica Center for Immigration Rights, the ACLU of Maryland and the National Immigration Project.

entries.title: Federal Judge Says DHS Acted ‘Capriciously’ When Halving FEMA’s Staff
entries.summary: The department gutted the contracts for CORE employees earlier this year without using “reasoned decisionmaking,” the judge wrote.
entries.content:
A federal judge in California sided with a labor union on Friday in its lawsuit against the Trump administration, saying the Department of Homeland Security “arbitrarily” moved to slash the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s staff by 50% earlier this year.

U.S. District Judge Susan Illston ruled that DHS acted “capriciously” when it revoked FEMA’s long-standing authority to renew contracts for its Cadre of On-Call Response/Recovery, or CORE employees. CORE employees are on-the-ground contacts who are dispatched across the country and remain in communities years after a disaster.

CORE employees have traditionally comprised around 40% of FEMA’s staff. Several workers previously told The Washington Sun that gutting the office would compromise essential recovery efforts in the aftermath of a disaster.

Illston said in her ruling that the government didn’t present any evidence that suggested DHS had used “reasoned decisionmaking” when conducting the mass firings.

“The record instead reflects that DHS was exempt from the President’s hiring freeze but then interpreted ‘new hires’ under the hiring freeze to include FEMA CORE term renewals,” Illston, a Clinton appointee, wrote. “The record also reflects that revoking FEMA’s CORE renewal authority impeded FEMA’s ability to perform its functions.”

Illston wrote that evidence in the case appeared to show the staffing cuts were helmed by former DHS leaders Joseph Guy and Kara Voorhies, as well as Karen Evans, who recently returned to the department to lead a fraud task force. Voorhies, who left her position as a FEMA contractor in the spring, has been under scrutiny by lawmakers from both parties for allegedly having an outsized role in managing FEMA contracts.

The court also found that Guy, Voorhies and Evans improperly used auto-delete features on the secure messaging application Signal to discuss staffing reductions.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Illston’s ruling.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Anthropic Founder Calls for AI Companies to Slow Progression
entries.summary: The technology’s rampant growth has been a major topic of discussion among lawmakers and industry leaders this week.
entries.content:
Dario Amodei, the co-founder of AI giant Anthropic, called for companies to slow the technology’s progression in an essay shared Saturday, citing growing potential for harm as the tool’s power grows.

Notably, Amodei’s essay called for companies to partner with the federal government, which could serve as an “evaluator” that implements safety regulations or as a mediator between tech corporations in the process of establishing standards. He also repeatedly invoked the word “democracy” in comparison to China, a longstanding competitor in the exploding industry that Cabinet members say poses a national security risk to U.S. infrastructure.

The CEO’s warning comes as congressional lawmakers and candidates argue about how best to rein in the technology, particularly while several proposals aimed at regulating AI have struggled to pass both chambers — leading some politicians to believe the federal government is missing a crucial window to establish guardrails.

Amodei’s essay follows viral messages from three industry workers this week — including a former Anthropic researcher — cautioning that AI’s “out of control” growth could soon lead to disastrous disruptions for society.

In his essay, Amodei said he’s become “convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence — not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.”

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei said. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

Amodei said the “accelerating rate of AI capability development” could potentially result in a swarm of AI agents “taking over the entire internet” within six to 12 months. By slowing down, he argued, technology companies could achieve “greater operational excellence,” reduce safety risks, enhance testing and evaluation and obtain greater understanding as to what “goes on inside these models.”

Amodei also urged maintaining stronger safety measures against China, which the company claimed in a report this week had used its models to conduct research that could have been used to generate biological weapons. The CEO called for the government and other tech companies to stop selling powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China, as well as curb chip smuggling operations.

Deputy CIA Director Michael Ellis also disclosed Tuesday in public remarks that the United States considers Chinese companies a legitimate target for espionage in fields such as artificial intelligence.

“Some may believe these measures make it more difficult to cooperate with China, but I believe the opposite is true,” Amodei wrote. “These measures increase the leverage held by democracies and make an agreement more likely in the future.”

President Donald Trump has called for the expansion of AI data centers, even as they grow more unpopular with the public, and further tech innovation to better compete with China. When asked if he was concerned about the former Anthropic researcher’s claims that AI could lead to human extinction on Thursday, the president said he didn’t have any worries.

“I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” Trump told reporters. “We are leading China right now by a pretty good period, I would say a year, which is, you know, considered a lot.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Amodei’s letter.

Other American AI leaders, including Elon Musk of xAI and Sam Altman of OpenAI, concurred with Amodei’s message on Saturday.

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said on X, adding that the idea had also been circulating at OpenAI this month. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We'll have more to share soon.”

Altman has met with Trump repeatedly throughout the president’s second term, including discussing plans for the government to acquire “pieces” of their firms in what would be among the most significant federal interventions in the private sector. The OpenAI founder also confirmed to Fortune on Friday that the company won’t be going public this year given the safety concerns, calling it an “ill-advised moment” to do so.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who sits on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, said the CEO’s ideas were a “reasonable start” that took into consideration “the proposition that we need real proposals that can be enacted rapidly.”

Earlier in the week, committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said he was working with Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) on legislation to address “catastrophic risks involving biological or nuclear threats.” Anthropic’s head of external affairs, Sarah Heck, said in an X post Saturday afternoon that the company is “eager” to work with lawmakers on their AI safety measures.

But, Cruz told Politico this week, slowing down would be an “impossible endeavor,” especially while competing with China.

“We could have government step in and shut down the AI industry in America. You know what would happen?” he said. “China would catch up in six months and soar ahead, and we wouldn’t have the tools to defend ourselves.”
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Burgum’s Arch Excavation Announcement Stirs Additional Legal Tensions
entries.summary: The Trump administration and a group of veterans disagreed whether Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s social media post violated a federal judge’s orders.
entries.content:
A group of veterans who legally challenged President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch pushed back against the administration’s request earlier this week to dissolve a court order that required 48 hours’ notice before engaging in any construction.

At the center of the legal battle’s newest phase is Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s Sept. 3 statement that groundbreaking for the arch would begin within the next two weeks — a social media announcement that the plaintiffs say violated the federal judge’s prior order for two weeks’ advance notice and created “consequences” for the government, a Friday court filing says.

The plaintiffs subsequently filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order to halt the work after Burgum shared his post on X. They argued that Burgum’s announcement ran afoul a previous court order from U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan that required the National Park Service to give at least 14 days’ notice prior to “commencement of construction, or demolition in preparation for construction” while litigation was pending.

Chutkan’s 48 hours’ notice — signed Sept. 4, a day after Burgum’s announcement — applied to activity such as excavation and construction, but exempted on-site information gathering to ensure compliance with the National Historic Preservation Act.

At the time, it was unclear whether the secretary’s social media post had constituted two weeks’ notice based on the first court order.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

In its motion to dissolve the 48 hours’ notice on Thursday, the Trump administration called it an “unlawful and unwarranted” hold on “routine agency actions that cause no harm to Plaintiffs and in the meanwhile disturbs the Executive Branch’s prerogatives to maintain property under its jurisdiction and control.”

The government also argued in its filing that the plaintiffs “manufactured a false emergency based on a misconstrued social media post” in order to stop excavation. Burgum’s announcement, the administration said, “simply summarized” plans that had been disclosed on the NPS’ website that required excavation to comply with legal statutes prior to construction.

In their response Friday, the veterans countered that the government was seeking to “avoid the consequences of Secretary Burgum’s announcements” and the “transparency” required by the 48 hours’ notice.

The veterans said they were “reasonably concerned that NPS was planning imminently to begin construction of the arch” and that the Trump administration “quickly backtracked” on Burgum’s statements after the temporary restraining order was filed.

“The Court’s order reasonably avoids the need for future emergency motions by ensuring that Defendants provide timely and accurate information about their steps to implement a massive and irreversible construction project that Plaintiffs contend has no legal foundation and that is rapidly progressing in the face of an active legal challenge,” the veterans’ filing read.

The arch is one of the many construction projects spearheaded by Trump to rework D.C. landmarks to match his gilded aesthetics. Like other projects, such as the White House ballroom and the redesign of a golf course, the arch has faced criticism from local residents and lawmakers for its scale.

The veterans sued the Trump administration in February, stating that the arch requires congressional approval and would obstruct the view of Arlington National Cemetery.
